- When sentiment is consistently neutral (0.00), model tends to overestimate early in horizon and underestimates late — adjust forecast to align with recent mean reversion.
- If sentiment is positive (≥0.20), model often overreacts to short-term spikes, overshooting true price — reduce forecast peak values by 5–10% after spike.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.00), model underestimates downward moves — increase forecast lows by 3–7% to account for potential rebound.
- Model frequently underestimates 30-day horizon in high-sentiment periods — apply upward bias of 1–3% to forecast tail end if sentiment > 0.10.
- If recent history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days trending down), model tends to lag — forecast should be adjusted upward 2–5% to catch reversal early.
- When sentiment is flat and history shows volatility, model often fails to capture volatility clustering — add 1–2% volatility buffer to forecast extremes.
